questions.title: Storage format on the backup dataset
questions.context: BKP-01 locks 'nightly job writes to a dedicated dedup-off dataset on the backup pool'. The existing backup/backups dataset has dedup=on (disko-config.nix), so a NEW dataset is needed regardless. Open question: what do the backup artifacts look like on it? Nightly payload is small (pg_dump + a dozen SQLite dumps, likely MBs to low GBs) on an 11 TB pool.

options.label: Plain dated directories
options.description: e.g. <dataset>/<service>/<date>/. Dumps land as ordinary files; restore is cp/sqlite3/pg_restore with zero extra tooling; human- and agent-greppable; ZFS lz4 compresses. Tradeoff: no cross-night dedup (full copies each night) — likely irrelevant at this payload size on this pool.

options.label: restic repository
options.description: Content-addressed dedup, encryption, and retention (forget --prune) built in; restic is already installed. Tradeoff: opaque repo (every restore needs restic), a repo password to manage in SOPS, and a heavier moving part for a local-only target.

options.label: Plain dirs + nightly zfs snapshot
options.description: Engine writes/overwrites a 'latest' tree; retention = ZFS snapshots of the dataset, pruned on schedule. History browsable via .zfs/snapshot; no new tools. Tradeoff: retention logic lives in ZFS-land; restore of older nights goes through snapshot paths, slightly less obvious than dated dirs.

questions.chat_more: We should have a sliding window for how long snapshots are retained. We can get remote backups working later, which can be used to store indefinitely.

questions.title: Orchestration shape
questions.context: The repo already splits per-service host modules under hosts/ser8/media/ and hosts/ser8/household/. The engine must cover ~12 services with 3 different methods (pg_dump, sqlite3 .backup, file copy).

options.label: Per-service systemd units + one nightly timer
options.description: backup-mealie.service, backup-sonarr.service, ... pulled in by a backup-nightly.target. Failures isolated per service; systemctl status is legible per app; matches the repo's per-service module layout. Tradeoff: more units to declare (mitigated by a Nix helper function).

options.label: Single orchestrator script/unit
options.description: One backup-nightly.service walking all services in sequence. One place to read the whole flow. Tradeoff: one failure blob (needs careful continue-on-error logic), one giant script, per-service status less visible to systemd/monitoring.

options.label: Nix module with per-service options
options.description: A homelab.backup.services.<name> = { method = "sqlite"; paths = [...]; } option set that generates the per-service units. Most idiomatic and reusable (future hosts, Phase 15 path changes become one-line edits). Tradeoff: most upfront design; risks over-abstraction for a single host — but Phase 15 WILL move paths, so declarative coverage pays off next phase.

questions.chat_more:
I like c, but doesn't need to be per-service option but per domain.

I'm not sure where this should be registered, either. The current flake structure isn't well-suited for flake-parts / modular options.

We also need to explore restore behavior -- this also makes me think, is there a flake / app / service that already supports this kind of workflow with a nice UI? 

Like backing up a sqlite db has nothing to do with the service that uses, we just generate a new backup service for the target.

We can also think about systemd targets here, like sshd-keygen uses for parameterized key generation targets.

questions.title: Nightly schedule and missed-run policy
questions.context: ser8 is busiest overnight: SABnzbd/NZBGet imports and Frigate camera writes run 24/7. systemd Persistent=true replays a missed run after downtime (relevant — ser8 reboots happen during phases).

options.label: Fixed 03:00 + Persistent=true
options.description: Simple, predictable, easy to reason about in logs and alerts. Tradeoff: may collide with overnight download/import churn (app-consistency is fine — dumps are transactional — it's just I/O contention).

options.label: 03:00 + RandomizedDelaySec + Persistent=true
options.description: Spreads I/O within a window to avoid a thundering herd of per-service units. Tradeoff: 'when did last night's backup run' becomes fuzzy by up to the delay window.

options.label: Planner picks the quiet window
options.description: Let the planner measure ser8's actual overnight I/O pattern (download schedules, Frigate churn) and pick the time. Tradeoff: one more research task, but grounded in evidence — matches the Phase 13 measured-data posture.

questions.title: Retention policy
questions.context: Retention interacts with Q-01 (dirs pruned by the engine vs snapshots vs restic forget). Payload is small, pool is 11 TB — space is not the constraint; recovery-window coverage is.

options.label: 14 nightlies, flat
options.description: Two weeks of point-in-time recovery, dead-simple pruning. Tradeoff: silent data corruption discovered after 2 weeks is unrecoverable.

options.label: GFS: 7 daily + 4 weekly + 6 monthly
options.description: Long tail for slow-burn problems (corrupted recipe found months later) at ~17 retained sets. Tradeoff: slightly more pruning logic (trivial with restic/zfs snapshot naming, manual-ish with plain dirs).

options.label: 30 nightlies, flat
options.description: A month of dailies, still simple pruning. Tradeoff: no long tail beyond 30 days; 2x the sets of option (a) for marginal gain over GFS.

questions.title: Fate of the stale backup scaffolding
questions.context: modules/servers/backup.nix (imported by ser8 via flake.nix) is a dead template: installs borg+restic+rsync, creates an unused 'backup' user, and ships a placeholder script to /etc/backup/. Repo philosophy: 'replace, don't deprecate'. Separately, the legacy backup/backups dataset (dedup=on, /mnt/backups) may hold manually-placed data — needs a live check before touching.

options.label: Delete template; leave legacy dataset alone
options.description: Remove the dead module (and its unused user) as part of this phase; new engine gets its own module. backup/backups stays as-is for manual use after verifying contents. Tradeoff: dedup=on lingers on a dataset the engine doesn't use — harmless but a standing footgun.

options.label: Delete template AND rationalize the legacy dataset
options.description: Also audit /mnt/backups contents, migrate anything real into the new layout, then flip dedup off (or retire the dataset). Cleanest end state, single backup surface. Tradeoff: touches live data — needs its own gated step and an inventory first.

options.label: Leave template in place
options.description: Ship the new engine alongside the old scaffolding. Tradeoff: violates the repo's no-dead-code stance; the placeholder script and unused user keep misleading future readers. Not recommended.

questions.title: Arr apps method (Sonarr/Radarr/Prowlarr/Bazarr)
questions.context: BKP-03 locks sqlite3 .backup + PRAGMA integrity_check for SQLite services; BKP-07 says 'correct method per state store'. The arr apps ALSO have a built-in Backup API (zip of DB + config.xml) — Phase 12 proved API access works and keys are in SOPS.

options.label: Direct sqlite3 .backup + config.xml copy
options.description: Uniform with every other SQLite service; works on the live DB via the backup API of sqlite itself (WAL-safe); no app API keys needed in the backup path. Tradeoff: bypasses the app's own blessed export; must enumerate the right .db files per app (sonarr.db, logs.db etc.) and keep that list current through Phase 15.

options.label: Built-in arr Backup API
options.description: App-consistent zip made by the app itself (DB + config), the restore path arr documentation describes. Tradeoff: internally it's the app's own DB copy (not your locked sqlite3 method — BKP-03 would need reading as 'SQLite-backed household services'); needs API keys wired into backup units; zip contents opaque to integrity_check.

options.label: Both
options.description: sqlite3 .backup for the locked-method guarantee plus the app zip for the app-blessed restore path. Tradeoff: double the artifacts and moving parts for four apps; restore drill should still pick ONE canonical path.

questions.chat_more:
Can we validate whether or not anything special is done by the arr apps when creating backups? I think its better to just integrate with the arr apps in this case; we use their APIs which may change backup behavior between releases, so better to not assume and cause silent drift between expected vs actual backup behavior.

We can still have a generic SQLite backup method for services that do not have bespoke backup implementation / behavior.

questions.title: Jellyfin backup scope
questions.context: /var/lib/jellyfin holds SQLite DBs (library, users, playback state), config, plus large re-fetchable metadata/artwork caches and transcode temp. DB+config is MBs; full state can be many GBs.

options.label: DBs + config only
options.description: sqlite3 .backup of the DBs plus the config dirs; exclude metadata/cache/transcodes. Small and fast; users/watch-state/library structure preserved. Tradeoff: restore triggers a metadata/artwork re-fetch and library re-scan (hours of background work, cosmetic gaps meanwhile).

options.label: Everything except cache/transcodes
options.description: DBs (via sqlite3 .backup) + config + metadata/artwork. Turnkey restore, no re-scan. Tradeoff: nightly working set jumps by GBs of mostly-static images; with plain dated dirs (Q-01a) that's GBs duplicated per night — really wants an incremental format (Q-01 b/c) to be sane.

questions.chat_more: I like (B), and this makes me think: Can dedup be an option in the backup module? Can we make it per-service?

questions.title: SABnzbd/NZBGet scope
questions.context: Both are config-file services (sabnzbd.ini, nzbget.conf — both contain secrets, both partly SOPS-templated already). Queues/history live in their state dirs; queue contents are transient downloads by design (D-21: failed/incomplete items are disposable).

options.label: Config files only
options.description: The reproducible-state position: config is the only thing that can't be regenerated (and much of it is already in the repo/SOPS); an in-flight queue lost in a restore just means re-grabbing. Smallest surface.

options.label: Config + history/queue state
options.description: Also capture download history DBs and queues (SABnzbd history1.db is SQLite → locked method applies). Restores preserve 'what was downloaded when' forensics and mid-flight queues. Tradeoff: nightly churn on files whose loss costs almost nothing.

questions.title: PostgreSQL dump strategy
questions.context: PostgreSQL 17 currently serves exactly one DB (Mealie, via database.createLocally). BKP-02 requires pg_dump of Mealie. Roles/globals live outside per-DB dumps.

options.label: pg_dump -Fc mealie only
options.description: Exactly the requirement; custom format is pg_restore-able with reordering/partial restore. Tradeoff: role/ownership globals not captured — scratch restore must recreate the mealie role first (fine: the NixOS module does this declaratively).

options.label: Per-DB pg_dump -Fc for ALL DBs + pg_dumpall --globals-only
options.description: Future-proof: any DB added later (Phase 15+ services) is covered automatically if the unit globs pg_databases; globals dump captures roles. Tradeoff: slightly more script; globals dump is near-trivial today.

options.label: pg_dumpall (everything, plain SQL)
options.description: One artifact, roles included. Tradeoff: plain-SQL only (no pg_restore selectivity), all-or-nothing restores, scales worst as DBs grow.

questions.title: Services beyond the named list (HA, Frigate, Mosquitto, Samba)
questions.context: The phase goal says 'Every stateful service on ser8'; the success criteria enumerate only household + media apps. Also stateful: Home Assistant (SQLite + .storage YAML), Frigate (frigate.db event index; recordings are media-content-class), Mosquitto (persistence db), Samba (user password tdb under /var/lib/samba/private).

options.label: Include all four now
options.description: Goal-literal. HA via sqlite3 .backup + .storage copy, frigate.db, mosquitto persistence, samba tdb export. Tradeoff: grows the phase surface ~30% and the restore-drill matrix; HA DB can be GBs of recorder history.

options.label: Named list only; document exclusions
options.description: Criteria-literal: ship the 11 named services, record HA/Frigate/Mosquitto/Samba as explicit, reasoned exclusions + a deferred follow-up. Tradeoff: 'every stateful service' isn't literally true this phase; HA state (automations, zigbee pairings in .storage) stays unprotected.

options.label: Add the cheap, irreplaceable ones: HA + Samba secrets
options.description: HA .storage + DB and the samba passdb are genuinely irreplaceable (pairings, credentials); frigate.db (rebuildable event index) and mosquitto (retained MQTT topics) are not. Middle path: +2 small units, skips the rebuildables with documented rationale.

questions.title: Partial failure semantics
questions.context: ~12 per-service backups per night. The failure mode that hurts: one flaky service silently costing you every OTHER service's backup for that night.

options.label: Independent: continue on failure, report per service
options.description: Each service backup succeeds/fails on its own; the night's run is 'partial' not 'absent'; alerting reports exactly which services failed. Natural fit with per-service units (Q-02 a/c).

options.label: Fail-fast: first error aborts the run
options.description: Loud and unambiguous — a red night forces immediate attention. Tradeoff: one broken app blanks all other services' recovery points for the night; effectively couples unrelated services.

questions.chat_more:
Can't we have a "parent" systemd backup service that spawns the independent child ones?

That way the failures are independent, but can be sent an alert / digest from the parent service (similar to how I get email alerts for ZFS now).

questions.title: Failure alerting channel
questions.context: Existing surfaces: ZED already emails catgrep@sudomail.com from ser8; firebat runs Prometheus + Alertmanager (email) scraping ser8's node exporter; no textfile collector is currently enabled. Project core value: 'I know about it before it becomes a problem.'

options.label: OnFailure email from ser8
options.description: systemd OnFailure= hook sending mail via the existing ser8 mail path. Immediate, no cross-host dependency. Tradeoff: catches loud failures only — a timer that silently never fires sends no email; no dashboard/history.

options.label: Freshness metric + firebat alert rule
options.description: node exporter textfile collector exports backup_last_success_timestamp per service; firebat alerts when any service's backup is >26h stale. Catches BOTH failures and silent never-rans; fits the established monitoring pattern; graphable. Tradeoff: needs textfile collector enablement; alert arrives on the next scrape, not instantly.

options.label: Both (recommended shape for the core value)
options.description: OnFailure email for immediate loud failures + freshness metric/alert as the safety net for silent ones. Tradeoff: two mechanisms to maintain — but they cover disjoint failure classes.

questions.title: Per-run verification depth
questions.context: BKP-03 already locks PRAGMA integrity_check on every SQLite backup. Question is what else each nightly run verifies about its own artifacts before declaring success.

options.label: Existence + size sanity
options.description: Artifact exists, non-empty, size within a tolerance band of the previous run. Catches truncated/empty dumps. Cheapest.

options.label: (a) + pg_restore --list on the pg dump
options.description: Also proves the PostgreSQL dump is structurally readable (the pg equivalent of integrity_check). Near-free; recommended baseline.

options.label: (a) + (b) + periodic automated test-restore
options.description: Monthly job restores one rotating service into a throwaway dir and sanity-checks it — backups are only real when restored. Tradeoff: real machinery; could equally be a deferred follow-up once the manual drills (BKP-05/06) have proven the paths.

questions.chat_more:
(a) + (b) is sufficient I think.

Not sure if its worth it to have an automated test running on the live system.

If anything, we should have VM tests for verifying this that can be run pre-deployment.

questions.title: Run manifest
questions.context: systemd/journald already captures per-unit logs. A manifest is a per-night machine-readable record ON the backup dataset itself (what was backed up, sizes, checksums, durations).

options.label: journald only
options.description: Zero extra artifacts; history lives in the journal (bounded retention). Tradeoff: at restore time — possibly on a dead or reinstalled host — the journal may be gone; the dataset alone doesn't say what a complete night looks like.

options.label: journald + per-night MANIFEST on the dataset
options.description: Self-describing backups: the restore-time picker ('what do I have, from when, is it complete') travels with the data; enables the size-band check (Q-13) and drift audits. Tradeoff: one more small artifact per night.

questions.title: Mealie scratch-restore mechanics (BKP-05)
questions.context: BKP-05: a Mealie restore into a scratch instance, demonstrated and documented. Mealie = Postgres DB + image/upload tree; the NixOS module can stand up both.

options.label: NixOS container on ser8
options.description: Declarative systemd-nspawn container (containers.mealie-scratch) with its own postgres + mealie on a scratch port; easy teardown; runs where the backups live. Tradeoff: container shares the host kernel/nix store — less of a 'bare metal died' rehearsal; ser8 gains a temporary container definition.

options.label: Second instance on ser8 (different port/state dir)
options.description: No container machinery — a parallel mealie-scratch service + scratch postgres cluster. Tradeoff: pollutes the host's service/state namespace, teardown is manual, easy to leave residue on an impermanence host (which does auto-clean unpersisted state on reboot — mildly self-correcting).

options.label: Local VM (nixos-rebuild build-vm) on the workstation
options.description: Fully isolated, closest rehearsal of real disaster recovery ('ser8 is gone, restore elsewhere from the backup pool'). Tradeoff: needs the backup artifacts copied off ser8 (itself a useful drill), and an x86 VM on the Apple-silicon workstation means emulation or a linux builder — the broken dev-machine remote-builder finding (Phase 11) is adjacent here.

questions.chat_more:
> Tradeoff: needs the backup artifacts copied off ser8 (itself a useful drill), and an x86 VM on the Apple-silicon workstation means emulation or a linux builder — the broken dev-machine remote-builder finding (Phase 11) is adjacent here.

We can use limactl / colima, there are other probably better options that can use apple's virtualization framework natively.

[Added via chat 2026-08-26] Reference repo using lima with Nix: ~/github/experiments/nix (readable from future sessions — operator added it to sagent extraReadPaths in flake.nix; restart the session to pick it up). Also research whether Determinate Nix's macOS linux-builder has matured (was experimental/poor when the operator last tried it) as an alternative to lima/colima for running the restore-drill VM.

questions.title: Which SQLite service for the BKP-06 restore demo
questions.context: BKP-06 requires demonstrating a restore of ONE SQLite-backed service (plus Actual, which is fixed). The choice sets which restore path gets battle-tested first.

options.label: Sonarr (or Radarr)
options.description: Validates the arr restore path — the one Phase 15's pre-cutover snapshot/rollback will actually lean on. Highest downstream value; medium-size DB with real history to verify against.

options.label: Donetick or Homebox
options.description: Smallest, most self-contained DBs; cheapest drill with the least at stake if the drill misbehaves. Tradeoff: proves the least about the harder restores.

options.label: Jellyfin
options.description: The scariest DB (users, watch state, library) — proving it restorable buys the most peace of mind and de-risks Phase 15's Jellyfin move. Tradeoff: most complex drill; multi-DB service.

questions.title: Restore path form
questions.context: The drills (BKP-05/06) will exercise whatever form this takes. Repo philosophy favors verification at every level and no speculative tooling.

options.label: Runbook only
options.description: A RESTORE doc with exact per-service steps, validated by executing them during the drills. Tradeoff: docs drift silently as paths/services change (Phase 15 will change paths); nothing executable to smoke-test.

options.label: Per-service restore scripts + short runbook
options.description: backup-restore-<service> scripts in the repo (the drills run THESE), runbook explains when/how to invoke. Scripts are shellcheck-linted, reviewable, and fail loudly when drift breaks them. Tradeoff: ~12 small scripts to maintain (or one script parameterized per service).

options.label: Single parameterized restore tool
options.description: One backup-restore <service> <date> entry point driven by the same per-service definitions as the backup units (pairs naturally with Q-02c). Symmetric with the engine, single source of truth for methods. Tradeoff: most design work; a bug is shared by all services.

questions.chat_more: We should research to see what's available for (c) -- this seems like a common feature to want.

questions.title: Restore documentation location
questions.context: Must survive milestone archiving (.planning/ artifacts get archived) and be findable during an actual incident. GSD terminology is banned outside .planning/ (D-23).

options.label: docs/ at repo root (e.g. docs/RESTORE.md)
options.description: Top-level, incident-findable, host-agnostic home; the repo currently has no docs/ dir — this starts one. Tradeoff: new top-level convention for a single doc.

options.label: hosts/ser8/README.md section
options.description: Colocated with the host the backups protect; README already documents host specifics. Tradeoff: buried for incident response; awkward if a restore ever targets a different host.

options.label: Module-adjacent (modules/backup/README.md)
options.description: Lives next to the engine code it documents; moves with the module. Tradeoff: less discoverable than repo-root docs during an incident.

questions.title: Module placement
questions.context: Established pattern from Phase 10 (recorded in STATE.md): reusable module + host-policy slice. Backup engine is currently ser8-only, but firebat has no snapshot-capable storage and ser8's backup pool is 'the fleet's only durable target' (Phase 09 decision).

options.label: modules/backup/ role group
options.description: Reusable engine module imported by ser8, like modules/media/ and modules/household/. Tradeoff: only one host will import it for the foreseeable future — reusability is speculative until a second host needs it.

options.label: hosts/ser8/backup/ host slice
options.description: Backup policy is inherently ser8-shaped (its pool, its services); matches the hosts/ser8/media/ per-service split. Tradeoff: if firebat state ever needs shipping to ser8's pool, engine code gets promoted later (cheap, mechanical).

options.label: Hybrid: engine in modules/, coverage in hosts/ser8/
options.description: The Phase 10 household pattern applied to backups: generic engine (units/timer/manifest generation) in modules/backup/, the per-service coverage list as ser8 host policy. Cleanest separation; pairs naturally with Q-02c. Tradeoff: two places to read; most structure for a one-host feature.

questions.title: Smoketest scope
questions.context: Repo rule: changed deployed services need smoketests; deploy.yaml drives area entry points (all.sh). The deferred-items table already records several always-pass smoketests as a known sore point — this phase should not add another.

options.label: New scripts/smoketests/backup/ area
options.description: all.sh + test-*.sh asserting: timer scheduled, last run succeeded, every covered service has an artifact fresher than 26h, spot integrity_check on one artifact, manifest complete. Wired into deploy.yaml. Full pattern-conformant coverage.

options.label: Fold into scripts/smoketests/ser8/
options.description: One test-backup.sh beside test-zfs-health.sh — fewer moving parts, no deploy.yaml change. Tradeoff: backup checks run only with the ser8 area; less granular failure output.

options.label: Minimal: timer-active check only
options.description: Cheapest possible check. Tradeoff: exactly the always-pass-adjacent shape the deferred-items table warns about — a scheduled timer whose runs all fail would still pass. Not recommended.

questions.title: ZFS auto-snapshots and the new backup dataset
questions.context: CORRECTED after live verification (2026-08-26): services.zfs.autoSnapshot is enabled in ser8's config but currently INERT — the NixOS tooling only snapshots datasets that opt in via com.sun:auto-snapshot=true, and no ser8 dataset does (live ser8 has zero auto-snapshots; the only 4 snapshots are manual: impermanence @blank, pre-26.05, and Phase 13's media/data@verified). So the question is whether the new backup dataset becomes the FIRST user of that machinery (opt in = a second retention layer over the engine's own) or stays out.

options.label: Engine owns retention; dataset stays out
options.description: Do not opt in (optionally set com.sun:auto-snapshot=false explicitly for clarity, matching cameras and media/data). Single retention authority, predictable space, deletions actually delete. The autoSnapshot config block stays dead — worth a cleanup note either way.

options.label: Opt in: auto-snapshots as an extra safety layer
options.description: Set com.sun:auto-snapshot=true on the new dataset — snapshots would protect backup artifacts against accidental deletion/tampering, and the dead config block gains its first real user. Tradeoff: two overlapping retention systems; engine pruning stops reclaiming space until snapshots age out; 15-min 'frequent' snapshots are pointless churn for a once-nightly dataset (per-interval opt-out properties like com.sun:auto-snapshot:frequent=false can restrict it, but that's more properties to manage).
